answer: ✅ Client-Facing Handout (Simple, No Jargon) A clean, friendly one-pager you can give to clients who ask about peptides. Peptides: What They Are, What They’re Not, and What You Should Know. What Are Peptides? Peptides are small chains of amino acids. Some are natural signals your body uses for healing, energy, hormones, or metabolism. A number of synthetic versions are being marketed for recovery, fat loss, and anti-aging. Most of them are NOT FDA-approved and have NOT been studied long-term in healthy people. What These Peptides Claim to Do: People use popular peptides because they believe they will help with: Faster injury healing; Better recovery; More energy; Fat loss; Improved hormones; Anti-aging. Some of these ideas come from animal studies or small human experiments. Most claims are not proven. The Big Risks You Should Know: Even if peptides sound “natural,” they come with real concerns: 1. Quality and purity vary a lot. Most peptides are made by compounders or online labs. Purity can be inconsistent. 2. Long-term safety is unknown. We don’t yet know how most peptides affect long-term health, hormones, or cancer risk. 3. Some peptides are banned in sports. For example, BPC-157 is prohibited for athletes. 4. Hormone-related peptides affect your body strongly. Peptides that raise growth hormone or sex hormones can affect blood sugar, swelling, nerves, or fertility. 5. Many require medical supervision. Some peptides are actually prescription drugs for specific medical conditions—not general fitness tools. The Most Important Thing: Whether you use peptides or not, the biggest improvements in health, fat loss, energy, and performance STILL come from: Eating the right amount of calories; Getting enough protein; Training consistently; Sleeping well; Managing stress; Moving more throughout the day. Peptides cannot replace these essentials. And they often work less than people expect unless the basics are already dialed in. If You’re Considering Peptides: Here’s the safest path: Talk to a qualified medical professional. Don’t buy peptides online or from unregulated sources. Get baseline labs (hormones, glucose, IGF-1, lipids). A doctor needs to know where you’re starting. Fix the basics first. Diet + training + sleep will give you 80–90% of the results. Use peptides—if at all—only as add-ons, not substitutes.

source_file: 2026/Peptides HRT, & GLP FAQs  -all-2026/Dosing Explanation.docx
filename: Dosing Explanation
answer:
Dosing Explanation. I want to clear up one of the most common points of confusion in the whole peptide space. It trips up beginners and people who have been at this for years. Hopefully, once it clicks, you'll never look at your syringe the same way. I get a version of this question almost every week. And unfortunately, I can't answer it. Well, even if I wanted to, I can’t answer this question. Why? Because that sentence tells me almost nothing. I’m probably as guilty as anyone for this gap in the marketplace, because when I created the peptide cheat sheet years ago, it gave people a way to introduce peptides without having to understand concrete math (BTW, you can download the most up-to-date version of the cheat sheet here). And today, I want to do my best, in writing, to explain how to always frame your communication about peptide dosages correctly. Let's get into it.

Unit Does Not = Dose. A unit is a measure of liquid, not a measure of peptide. Your insulin syringe is marked in units because that is how it reads off volume. The standard syringe holds 100 units per milliliter. So, 10 units is one-tenth of a milliliter of liquid. That's all the number means. The syringe has no idea what is dissolved in that liquid. It could be a tiny dose. It could be a huge one. The syringe can't tell, and neither can I, just from the unit number.

Don’t Skip This. So, what decides the actual dose? It’s how much water you put in the vial. The amount of bacteriostatic water you use to mix your peptide completely changes the amount of peptide per unit. Let me show you with real numbers. Say you have a 10mg vial of Retatrutide. You add 2ml of bacteriostatic water to it. That gives you 5mg per ml. Written another way, that's 5000mcg per ml. Your syringe holds 100 units per ml. Divide it out, and each unit carries 50 mcg. Pull 10 units, and you just dosed 500 mcg or 0.5 mg. Now here's where it gets interesting. Take that exact same 10mg vial. This time, mix it with only 1ml of water. Now you have 10mg per ml. Each unit contains 100 mcg instead of 50 mcg. The same 10 units now deliver 1mg. Same vial. Same 10 units on the syringe. DOUBLE the dose. That's why "10 units" means nothing on its own. Without the reconstitution ratio, you have no idea what you took.

The Math. Concentration equals the mg in your vial divided by the ml of water you added. Dose per unit equals that concentration divided by 100. That's it. Run those two lines on any vial and you'll always know exactly what one unit is worth. So, if a 10mg vial gets 2ml of water, that's 5mg per ml, and 0.05mg per unit. 50mcg. Want 250mcg? That's 5 units. Once you think this way, you stop asking how many units to take. You start by asking how many mcg or mg you're after, then do the quick math to get there. Different vials, different water volumes, and different goals all change the answer. Always confirm the mg in your specific vial before you mix, since a 5mg and a 10mg vial look identical once they're reconstituted. And if you're ever unsure, mix with a clean, round number like 2 ml. It makes the math easy and keeps you from guessing. Here’s a visual guide to help understand.

Final Thoughts. The unit number on your syringe is a volume readout. Nothing more. The people who get into trouble are the ones treating it like a dose. They copy "10 units" from someone else's recommendation without realizing the person used a different vial size or a different amount of water. Same number on the syringe, completely different reality in the body. Learn to think in mg and mcg. Let the units be what they are, a way to measure the liquid. Do that, and you'll always know what you're putting in your body.

source_file: 2026/Peptides HRT, & GLP FAQs  -all-2026/Epithalon,StimulatingTelomeraseIncreaseTelomereLength&AO,.docx
filename: Epithalon,StimulatingTelomeraseIncreaseTelomereLength&AO,
answer: Epitalon, a synthetic tetrapeptide (Ala-Glu-Asp-Gly), operates through multiple mechanisms at the cellular and genetic levels, most notably by stimulating the enzyme telomerase to increase telomere length. It also functions as an antioxidant, regulates the endocrine system (specifically melatonin production), and modulates gene expression. Key mechanisms of action include: Telomerase Activation and Telomere Elongation: Epitalon induces the expression and activity of the telomerase enzyme, which adds repetitive DNA sequences (telomeres) to the ends of chromosomes. This action helps prevent telomere shortening, a key biomarker of aging, thereby extending the proliferative capacity and lifespan of normal somatic cells in in vitro studies. Melatonin Secretion Regulation: The peptide acts on the pineal gland to restore and normalize age-related declines in melatonin production, which in turn helps regulate circadian rhythms and improve sleep patterns. Antioxidant Effects: Epitalon acts as a potent antioxidant, directly scavenging reactive oxygen species (free radicals) and also stimulating the expression of endogenous antioxidant enzymes (like superoxide dismutase). This activity reduces oxidative stress and cellular damage associated with aging and age-related diseases. Gene Expression Modulation (Epigenetic Mechanism): Epitalon has been shown to interact with histone proteins in chromatin, an epigenetic mechanism that can influence the transcription of various genes, including those involved in cellular differentiation, neurogenesis, immune function, and the suppression of tumor formation. Immune System Modulation: Research indicates that epitalon can help regulate immune function by influencing mediators such as cytokines and enhancing immune cell activity, potentially counteracting age-related immune system decline. Through these interconnected mechanisms, epitalon contributes to overall cellular health, tissue repair, and the potential delay of age-related diseases, as demonstrated in various preclinical and some early human studies.

source_file: 2026/Peptides HRT, & GLP FAQs  -all-2026/IGF-1 LR3 peptide info.docx
filename: IGF-1 LR3 peptide info
answer: IGF-1 LR3 (Long R3 Insulin-Like Growth Factor-1) is a synthetic analog of IGF-1 designed to have a much longer half-life and greater biological activity than natural IGF-1. It has an added 13-amino acid extension and a modification at the 3rd amino acid position, which reduces binding to IGF-binding proteins and allows it to remain active in circulation far longer. Its primary mechanism of action is direct activation of the IGF-1 receptor on muscle and other tissues, stimulating anabolic signaling pathways such as PI3K/Akt/mTOR and MAPK. These pathways increase protein synthesis, satellite cell activation, muscle cell proliferation, glucose uptake, tissue repair, and recovery while also reducing protein breakdown. The primary uses of IGF-1 LR3 are typically related to: Supporting lean muscle growth and recovery. Enhancing tissue repair after intense training or injury. Improving nutrient partitioning and body composition. Research into muscle regeneration, metabolism, and anabolic signaling. Because IGF-1 signaling also influences cellular growth broadly throughout the body, there are important safety considerations, including potential effects on blood glucose regulation and theoretical concerns regarding abnormal cell proliferation. Most legitimate clinical discussions emphasize medical supervision and careful monitoring. Dosage: There is no medically established or FDA-approved dosing protocol for IGF-1 LR3 in healthy individuals for muscle growth or performance enhancement. Most dosing information comes from experimental use, peptide clinics, and bodybuilding communities rather than large controlled human trials. That said, the most commonly referenced "performance-support" dosing ranges are: 20–50 mcg daily as a conservative/common range. 50–100 mcg daily in more aggressive experimental protocols. Typical cycle lengths discussed are 4–6 weeks, followed by time off to reduce receptor desensitization risk. The rationale behind these doses is to activate IGF-1 receptors enough to increase: muscle protein synthesis, satellite cell activation, recovery, and nutrient uptake, without excessively increasing side effects such as hypoglycemia, edema, nerve compression symptoms, or unwanted tissue growth. NEXGEN dosing: After 6 weeks we will assess progress (subjective) and decide if an IGF-1 LR3 peptide add is warranted. IGF-1 LR3 (5/6 weeks, 50–100µ daily; 1mg=20 50µ shots/vial [25units/shot]) 1vial=1mg (1000µ). Primary Use: Promotes muscle growth, recovery, and nutrient partitioning through direct anabolic signaling. Often considered one of the most potent downstream mediators of growth hormone activity. Mechanism: A modified long-acting IGF-1 analog that binds directly to IGF-1 receptors, stimulating protein synthesis, satellite cell activation, muscle tissue growth, and cellular recovery through activation of the Akt/mTOR anabolic pathway. Unlike GH secretagogues, it bypasses the pituitary and acts directly at the tissue level. (Note: Unlike Tesamorelin or Sermorelin, IGF-1 LR3 does not increase natural growth hormone production—it acts downstream of GH by directly activating IGF-1 pathways). Mechanistically, IGF-1 LR3 primarily works through the Akt/mTOR anabolic signaling pathway: A major concern with higher or prolonged dosing is that IGF-1 signaling is not muscle-specific — it can stimulate growth pathways in many tissues. Because of that, most medically oriented sources recommend conservative exposure, short durations, and monitoring of: fasting glucose, insulin sensitivity, IGF-1 blood levels, and general metabolic markers.

source_file: 2026/Peptides HRT, & GLP FAQs  -all-2026/KPV peptdie -skin -gut inflammation-immune system.docx
filename: KPV peptdie -skin -gut inflammation-immune system
answer:
KPV is a short tripeptide made of three amino acids—lysine, proline, and valine. It is the natural C-terminal fragment of alpha-melanocyte-stimulating hormone (α-MSH). KPV is studied for its potential anti-inflammatory and antimicrobial properties—aiming to soothe gut and skin inflammation without causing the skin-pigment changes linked to its parent hormone. [1, 2, 3]

How KPV Works in Research

Cellular signaling: Preclinical studies show KPV helps block NF-κB, a master protein complex that switches on inflammatory genes.

Cytokine reduction: Laboratory models demonstrate it lowers the production of pro-inflammatory chemicals like TNF-α, IL-6, and IL-1β.

Targeted absorption: In gut models, KPV is proposed to enter intestinal cells through the PepT1 peptide transporter, which is often more active during inflammation. [1, 2, 3]

Proposed Uses and Formulations

Gut health: Marketed or researched for conditions like inflammatory bowel disease or intestinal permeability ("leaky gut") via oral formats.

Skin conditions: Applied topically in creams or gels for local issues like eczema, psoriasis, or general redness.

Systemic inflammation: Sometimes compounded into nasal sprays or injectables. [1, 2, 3]

Safety and Regulatory Status

Lack of human trials: Almost all current data relies on cell cultures and animal models; large-scale safety and efficacy trials in humans are lacking. [1]

Regulation: KPV is not FDA-approved as a prescription medication. Products sold online or through wellness clinics often exist in a regulatory gray market as experimental research compounds, meaning purity, dosing accuracy, and sterility can vary significantly. [1, 2]

source_file: 2026/Peptides HRT, & GLP FAQs  -all-2026/KissPeptin,StimGnRH,secretionByGnRH neuron.docx
filename: KissPeptin,StimGnRH,secretionByGnRH neuron
answer:
Kisspeptin works by binding to its receptor on neurons in the hypothalamus, which stimulates the release of gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH). This begins a cascade: GnRH then signals the pituitary gland to release luteinizing hormone (LH) and follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH), which in turn stimulate the gonads (ovaries or testes) to produce sex hormones like estrogen, progesterone, and testosterone. This process is crucial for reproduction, puberty, and the menstrual cycle.

The chain of command

Kisspeptin starts the signal: Kisspeptin is a peptide hormone that acts on neurons in the hypothalamus.

GnRH is released: When kisspeptin binds to the KISS1R receptor on these neurons, it triggers the release of GnRH.

LH and FSH are released: GnRH travels to the pituitary gland, which then releases LH and FSH.

Sex hormones are produced: LH and FSH travel to the ovaries or testes, stimulating them to produce and release sex hormones such as estrogen, progesterone, and testosterone.

Key roles in reproduction

Puberty: Kisspeptin signaling is essential for the onset of puberty.

Menstrual cycle: It helps regulate the release of eggs from the ovary and is involved in the normal control of ovulation.

Fertility: It is a key regulator of the reproductive axis and is essential for fertility.

Other functions: Kisspeptin is also involved in a variety of other processes, including the integration of reproductive hormones with brain activity related to emotions and mood

filename: Mitochondria derived proteins-peptides
answer:
What is the process of mitochondria derived proteins, formerly called Mitochondria derived peptides?
Mitochondria-derived proteins (MDPs), formerly called mitochondria-derived peptides, are a relatively newly recognized group of small signaling proteins that are actually encoded within the mitochondrial genome itself. For decades, scientists believed mitochondria only encoded 13 proteins involved in energy production. We now know mitochondria also produce several small bioactive proteins that function almost like hormones or cellular “stress messengers.”
The process works roughly like this:
Mitochondrial DNA transcription
Mitochondria contain their own small circular DNA separate from nuclear DNA. Within regions once thought to be “non-coding,” small open reading frames (sORFs) are transcribed into RNA.
Translation into small proteins
These RNAs are translated by mitochondrial or sometimes cytoplasmic ribosomes into tiny proteins, usually under ~100 amino acids long. Examples include:
Humanin
MOTS-c
SHLPs (Small Humanin-Like Peptides)
Stress sensing and signaling
Production often increases during:
Exercise
Caloric restriction
Oxidative stress
Fasting
Mitochondrial dysfunction
The mitochondria essentially “report” cellular energy status to the rest of the cell and body.
Cellular and systemic actions
These proteins can leave the mitochondria and sometimes even circulate in blood, acting on distant tissues. Their actions include:
Improving insulin sensitivity
Enhancing glucose uptake
Supporting mitochondrial biogenesis
Reducing oxidative stress
Protecting neurons
Reducing inflammation
Supporting muscle metabolism and exercise adaptation
Communication with the nucleus
One of the most interesting features is “retrograde signaling,” where mitochondria communicate back to the nucleus to influence gene expression related to:
Longevity
Stress resistance
Metabolism
Cellular repair
One of the most studied examples is MOTS-c:
MOTS-c appears to activate metabolic pathways similar to exercise and energy stress, particularly the AMPK pathway, helping cells shift toward better glucose utilization and fat oxidation.
Another is Humanin, which has attracted major attention for:
neuroprotection,
anti-apoptotic effects,
and potential roles in healthy aging and diseases like Alzheimer’s.
The reason the terminology shifted from “peptides” to “proteins” is largely scientific refinement. Initially, these molecules were discovered as very short amino acid chains and called peptides. As understanding evolved, researchers recognized they behave more like true signaling proteins with endocrine-like functions, broader biological actions, and regulated expression patterns.
From a health and performance standpoint, MDPs are now being heavily investigated in:
aging and longevity,
insulin resistance,
obesity,
exercise adaptation,
neurodegeneration,
muscle preservation,
and recovery from metabolic stress.
One of the major emerging concepts is that exercise, proper nutrition, sleep, and metabolic health may partly exert their anti-aging and performance effects by improving mitochondrial signaling and increasing beneficial MDP activity.

source_file: 2026/Peptides HRT, & GLP FAQs  -all-2026/PUO and RUO product def -research & physician use.docx
filename: PUO and RUO product def -research & physician use
answer:
In the peptide manufacturing industry, RUO and PUO are designations used by suppliers to indicate the intended use, regulatory status, and manufacturing quality of a product. [1, 2, 3]
RUO (Research Use Only)
RUO means the product is intended strictly for in vitro laboratory research, in vivo animal studies, or early-stage drug discovery. [1, 2]
Manufacturing & Regulation: These products are generally exempt from the Food and Drug Administration's (FDA) rigid premarket clearance and cGMP (Current Good Manufacturing Practice) requirements for human pharmaceuticals. [1, 2]
Testing & Purity: While they are synthesized for chemical purity, they are not produced under the strict safety protocols, sterility, or viral-clearance standards required for human medications. [1, 2]
Legality: RUO peptides are legal to purchase and possess for scientific purposes, but it is illegal to market, prescribe, or administer them for human consumption. [1, 2]
PUO (Physician / Provider Use Only)
PUO is a relatively newer, distributor-level label intended to market peptides exclusively to licensed medical clinics or practitioners. [1]
The Intent: Suppliers often use this label to imply a higher standard of legitimacy or oversight compared to the direct-to-consumer RUO market. [1]
The Reality: From a regulatory perspective, PUO and RUO are legally treated the same. Unless a peptide is manufactured in an FDA-registered facility as an Active Pharmaceutical Ingredient (API) or an approved prescription drug, the PUO label does not automatically make the compound safe, legal, or compliant for human injection. [1, 2]
Key Takeaway for Safety and Sourcing
Neither RUO nor PUO signify that a peptide is a clinical-grade drug. True pharmaceutical-grade peptides must be produced under cGMP (Current Good Manufacturing Practices). You can verify legitimate drug manufacturers and FDA compliance by checking the FDA Drug Database. To understand the difference between research-grade and clinical manufacturing protocols, visit the FDA Guidance on RUO Labeling

Peptide Cheat Sheet (Quick Summary + Mechanism)
1. TB-500 (Thymosin Beta-4 Fragment)
Primary Use: Supports tissue repair, recovery, and reduced inflammation, commonly used for healing injuries or improving mobility.
Mechanism: Enhances actin polymerization, increases angiogenesis, and promotes cell migration, accelerating wound repair and reducing fibrosis.

Primary Use: Improves mitochondrial efficiency, energy production, and metabolic flexibility (fat oxidation, insulin sensitivity).

4. SS-31 (Elamipretide)
Primary Use: Protects the mitochondria, improves energy production, and reduces oxidative stress, investigated for heart, muscle, and age-related disorders.
Mechanism: Selectively binds cardiolipin in the inner mitochondrial membrane, stabilizing the ETC and reducing ROS leakage to boost ATP output.
5. AOD-9604 (Fragment of HGH 176-191)
Primary Use: Promotes fat loss without raising IGF-1 or causing GH-like systemic effects; often positioned for "stubborn fat" reduction.
Mechanism: Stimulates lipolysis and inhibits lipogenesis through the β-adrenergic and adenylate cyclase–cAMP pathways, independent of GH receptor activation.
6. Epitalon (Epithalamin / Epithalon)
Primary: Longevity-focused; supports sleep, circadian rhythm, and theoretical anti-aging effects.
Mechanism: Upregulates telomerase activity, supports pineal gland signaling, and helps regulate melatonin secretion and circadian timing.
7. Kisspeptin-10 / Kisspeptin-54
Primary Use: Enhances natural reproductive hormone output, often used for improving LH/FSH production, fertility, and libido.
Mechanism: Stimulates GnRH release from the hypothalamus, which increases LH → testosterone/estrogen production along the HPG axis.
8. Sermorelin*
Primary use: Restore the body's ability to release GH to support recovery, body composition, and healthy aging, more subtle and long-term.
Mechanism: Binds to GHRH receptors in the anterior pituitary to increase GH pulsatility (especially during sleep) to support anabolic signaling without suppressing natural GH production.
9. Tesamorelin
Primary Use: Increases natural growth hormone release and reduces visceral fat (FDA-approved for HIV-associated lipodystrophy). Step above Sermorelin, with stronger metabolic activity including GH signaling.
Mechanism: Acts as a potent GHRH analog that binds GHRH receptors, increasing pulsatile GH and subsequently raising lipolysis and IGF-1 levels.
10. Ibutamoren (MK-677) Oral non-peptide GH stimulant1
Primary use: To increase the body's natural growth hormone and IGF-1 levels to support muscle growth, recovery, and overall anabolic function without injections.
Mechanism: Mimics ghrelin ("hunger hormone") to activate ghrelin receptors (GHS-R1a), which signals the hypothalamus and pituitary to increase natural GH pulse release; liver then produces more IGF-1 leading to an increase in protein synthesis and reduction in muscle breakdown.
11. CJC-1295 (With or Without DAC)
Primary Use: Enhances natural GH/IGF-1 production for recovery, body composition improvements, and sleep quality.
Mechanism: Mimics growth hormone–releasing hormone (GHRH), amplifying GH pulse amplitude and duration, especially prolonged when DAC is included.
12. IGF-1 LR3
Primary Use: Promotes muscle growth, recovery, and nutrient partitioning through direct anabolic signaling. Often considered one of the most potent downstream mediators of growth hormone activity.
Mechanism: A modified long-acting IGF-1 analog that binds directly to IGF-1 receptors, stimulating protein synthesis, satellite cell activation, muscle tissue growth, and cellular recovery through activation of the Akt/mTOR anabolic pathway. Unlike GH secretagogues, it bypasses the pituitary and acts directly at the tissue level. (Note: Unlike Tesamorelin or Sermorelin, IGF-1 LR3 does not increase natural growth hormone production; it acts downstream of GH by directly activating IGF-1 pathways).
* Sermorelin: A shorter-acting GHRH peptide than Tesamorelin, that also stimulates GH release, but results can be less consistent and protocols vary
1 Ibutamoren (MK-677) is a small-molecule, non-peptide compound, specifically an orally active ghrelin receptor (GHS-R1a) agonist. It's a synthetic, drug-like molecule (not a chain of amino acids like peptides designed to bind the ghrelin receptor and stimulate GH release. Its small-molecule structure is what allows it to be taken orally and remain stable in the body. Therefore MK-677 works like a drug, not a peptide, so you can take it orally and it still activates the GH pathway effectively.

filename: Peptide status and good info-LA Times
answer: http://enewspaper.latimes.com/infinity/article_share.aspx?guid=009bf5cb-fc27-4d27-b98e-b76371fbb918 Unregulated peptide use alarms researchers. Consumer demand driven by online hype and distrust of health guidance. [NAME], a USC gerontologist, is concerned about the online marketing of his peptide discovery. (Christina House Los Angeles Times) By [NAME]. A few months ago, [NAME] learned of a thriving online trade in MOTS-c, a peptide that, when injected into mice, seems to mimic the effects of exercise. The dean of the USC Leonard Davis School of Gerontology was very familiar with this particular short chain of amino acids. His lab identified it years ago as one of the thousands of peptides that act as chemical messengers in the human body, one he believed might someday have therapeutic uses for humans. But [NAME] was alarmed to learn that his discovery was being promoted by legions of longevity seekers, fitness enthusiasts and wellness influencers as “exercise in a bottle.” Though not approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration, it was widely available online, often in vials marked “for research use only.” “Turns out that tens of thousands of people are injecting themselves with MOTS-c [that’s] black market, illegal, from unknown sources, unknown purity, unknown sterility, and I strongly object to that,” [NAME] said. Driven by social media hype and a growing distrust of public health guidance, consumer demand for experimental peptides has exploded over the last decade. Now, the clamor over unregulated peptides is fueling a high-stakes policy battle within the federal government. Health and Human Services Secretary [NAME] has described himself as a “big fan” and user of peptides and has pledged to end the government’s “aggressive suppression” of them. Some peptides, such as insulin, human growth hormone and glucagon-like peptide-1, have delivered transformational therapeutic effects when administered to humans. But every vial of insulin or GLP-1 medication on a pharmacist’s shelf is the product of decades of clinical trials and safety testing. There are reams of data on what these drugs do, for whom they are most effective and in what dose and form they should be administered. For MOTS-c and a raft of other peptides widely available online, no comparable evidence exists. Although proponents say the substances help with weight loss, energy and muscle mass, and often cite research that has been done solely on animals or on a very small number of humans, no one knows for certain how or when it should be used in humans. While many users take multiple peptides together in custom combinations, or “stacks,” there is no data on how different synthetic peptides interact with one another. To date, most of these popular peptides have been available solely in unregulated online marketplaces. But recently, an FDA committee voted to recommend that compounding pharmacies be allowed to manufacture six different peptides already widely available online: BPC-157, TB-500, KPV, epitalon, Semax and MOTS-c. A seventh, emideltide, was voted down. Compounding pharmacies, which mix bespoke drugs, are a loophole in the U.S. regulatory system. Though the drugs they produce aren’t FDA-approved, the pharmacies still have to follow their state’s safety and quality regulations. [NAME] traveled to Washington, D.C., to speak before the committee, many of whose members work for the kind of telehealth, longevity and wellness companies that stand to benefit financially from the peptides’ regulation. Given that MOTS-c already is widely used off-label and no research has shown evidence of harmful side effects, [NAME] said in his remarks that he believed “quality-controlled, prescriber-supervised” compounding was the safest way forward. “We can’t stop the black market. So I think it’s a better choice to at least guarantee the quality, the sterility, and require that real doctors are part of the process,” he said later. “I really think this is a better choice than just letting it go on the way it is.” Not everyone agrees with him. FDA staff who spoke at the two-day meeting advised against peptide compounding, saying there was not enough safety data to justify the move. The vote is non-binding, and the FDA could choose to side with its own scientists. “My impression is that the ‘lesser of two evils’ argument is a minority perspective,” said [NAME], a cell biology and human anatomy professor at the UC Davis School of Medicine who writes on peptides. “While it’s true that most compounders can likely [produce] purer versions of these peptides than what’s in the gray market, that doesn’t address potential inherent risks of the peptides themselves,” [NAME] said. “There’s no special reason they should be allowed to bypass the standard clinical trial system just because there’s a peptide fad driven by wellness influencers and telehealth firms.” [NAME] found MOTS-c by combing through the 97% of human DNA that doesn’t encode for genes. This biological hoard once dismissed as “junk DNA” or the “dark genome” has turned out to be full of hormones and microproteins that play important roles in directing the body’s systems and processes. Roughly 250 papers from dozens of research labs around the world have been published on MOTS-c since [NAME]’s lab identified it. While the peptide’s risks and side effects are few, and its effects on mouse metabolism compelling, no one knows how long-term use affects humans yet, or what formula or dosage would be most effective. Influencers’ claims about the peptides’ effect on human weight loss, muscle mass, longevity and energy appear to be extrapolated from their effects on lab animals. “Certain groups of people, for example, the fitness enthusiasts, which is the kind way to refer to gym rats, those people take one figure from one paper done on mice and take it to become gospel,” [NAME] said. Many users have been happy to essentially volunteer themselves for further testing. “Today I used Mots-c for the first time and I’m a believer,” a Reddit user posted this year. “I did some outdoor sports for about an hour and then came home and spent several hours doing every chore that had been piling up all week.” The reality is more nuanced. For scientists like [NAME], these molecules are an exciting area of research that could reap significant health breakthroughs. But rigorous science takes time, and they’re up against a public that has lost patience with the traditional drug approval model, and a market that is happy to provide alternatives. In an ideal world, [NAME] said, he would like to see MOTS-c developed into an FDA-approved drug. But in the actual world, taking a single drug from the lab to the market requires so much time (at least 10 years, usually more) and money (at least hundreds of millions of dollars, usually more) that very few candidates successfully reach that goal. His own efforts to move MOTS-c through the development pipeline stalled. “Peptides are neither miracle cures nor snake oil. They are signaling molecules. Some have strong evidence. Some have intriguing or early data. Some are wildly overhyped, and some probably should never leave the laboratory,” Dr. Ben Gonzalez, a former emergency medicine physician at Walter Reed Army Medical Center, said at the FDA meeting. “Patients are looking for alternatives, and they are looking not at physicians. They’re looking at this gray market source.” If compounded peptides ultimately are approved, [NAME] would like to start an online registry in which patients can anonymously record the dosage they’re taking, the reason they’re taking it and any side effects they experience, so scientists can collect data on this real-world experiment. “The big picture is that we’re transitioning as a nation from the 20th century model [in which] all healthcare was dictated by physicians and insurance companies to a new 21st century model where consumers are demanding and receiving health and wellness services and products that they pay for in cash,” [NAME] said. “I’m not saying that’s a better model. But it’s the model we’re transitioning into.”

answer:
General scientific consensus

Buccal delivery of peptides is scientifically plausible, but ordinary dissolving strips should not be assumed to deliver a therapeutically meaningful or reliable dose. The buccal cavity avoids stomach acid, intestinal enzymes, and some first-pass liver metabolism. However, the cheek lining remains an effective biological barrier, particularly against molecules that are relatively large, water-soluble, and electrically charged, which describes most therapeutic peptides. Reviews consistently identify low permeability, enzymatic degradation in saliva and mucosal tissue, short contact time, swallowing of the dose, and substantial person-to-person variability as major obstacles.

Therefore, the consensus is closer to:

Buccal peptide delivery is a promising drug-delivery research platform, but it is not a generally validated substitute for injection unless the specific peptide and finished formulation have demonstrated human pharmacokinetics and clinical efficacy.

A strip can dissolve in the mouth without the peptide actually crossing the mucosa. Much of the dissolved material may simply be swallowed and then degraded.

What is needed for a strip to work?

Successful formulations generally require more than putting peptide powder into a dissolvable film. Research systems often combine several technologies:
- A mucoadhesive polymer that keeps the drug against the cheek.
- A permeation enhancer, such as a surfactant, bile salt, fatty-acid derivative, cyclodextrin, chitosan, or cell-penetrating peptide.
- Protection from enzymatic degradation.
- Precise control of peptide stability, concentration, film dissolution, pH and contact time.
- Sometimes nanoparticles, liposomes, chemical peptide modification or directional films that prevent drug loss into saliva.

Even with these measures, exposure is often low or variable.

Are there supporting studies?

Yes, but most support the concept rather than proving that currently marketed wellness strips work.

Insulin

Insulin is the most studied example. A small proof-of-concept human study of an oral/buccal insulin spray reported reductions in post-meal glucose, demonstrating that some biologically active insulin could be delivered through the oral cavity. However, results with buccal insulin systems have generally shown variable absorption, and no conventional insulin cheek strip has become an established replacement for injected insulin.

More recent insulin research frequently involves sophisticated carriers or cell-penetrating peptides rather than a simple dissolving strip. For example, a 2020 study found improved buccal insulin transport using a specialized cell-penetrating-peptide system, but this was preclinical formulation research, not proof that an ordinary retail strip produces equivalent systemic exposure in humans.

Calcitonin

Salmon calcitonin has also been investigated because it is a potent peptide active at comparatively small doses. Studies using penetratin-conjugated liposomes have demonstrated improved buccal permeation, but the evidence has largely been in vitro or ex vivo, rather than large clinical outcome trials.

Other peptides

Laboratory and animal research has examined buccal delivery of insulin, calcitonin, TRH and other peptides, often showing that absorption can be increased using penetration enhancers. These findings establish biological feasibility, but they cannot automatically be extrapolated to BPC-157, CJC-1295, ipamorelin, TB-500, sermorelin or similar wellness peptides.

Regarding BPC-157, CJC-1295, ipamorelin and similar strips

I could not find credible published human pharmacokinetic trials demonstrating that commercially marketed buccal strips containing these peptides produce:
- Predictable blood concentrations,
- A stated percentage of absolute bioavailability,
- Comparable exposure to injection, or
- Clinically meaningful outcomes.

Claims such as “90% or 92% bioavailability” should be treated cautiously unless the seller can provide a peer-reviewed human crossover study comparing the finished strip with an intravenous or subcutaneous reference product. A company’s dissolution test, ingredient assay, testimonial or general research on buccal technology does not establish systemic bioavailability for its product.

This concern is separate from whether the peptide itself works. For several commonly marketed compounds, including BPC-157, CJC-1295 and ipamorelin, the FDA has cited limited safety information, peptide-related impurity concerns and potential immunogenicity issues.

Practical conclusion

The delivery route is credible in principle, but most peptide strips currently being promoted are ahead of the supporting clinical science. A properly engineered buccal pharmaceutical may deliver a particular peptide, especially a small and highly potent one. But efficacy is molecule- and formulation-specific; it cannot be inferred merely because a strip is placed against the cheek.

For evaluating a particular product, I would ask the manufacturer for:
- Human pharmacokinetic data on the finished strip, not just the raw peptide.
- Absolute or relative bioavailability with a clearly identified comparator.
- Blood concentration curves: Cmax, Tmax and AUC.
- Independent potency, purity and stability testing.
- Evidence that the dose remains intact through its expiration date.
- Published human clinical outcomes at the strip’s actual dose.

Without those data, the most scientifically accurate description is experimental and unproven, rather than demonstrably ineffective, but it should not be presented as comparable to injection.

answer: SS-31's mechanism of action involves a specific targeting of mitochondria, where it binds to a molecule called cardiolipin on the inner mitochondrial membrane. This interaction stabilizes the mitochondrial cristae, boosts ATP production, reduces oxidative stress by inhibiting cytochrome c peroxidase activity, and improves electron transport chain function. These actions protect against mitochondrial dysfunction and support overall cellular health. Key aspects of SS-31's mechanism: Mitochondrial targeting: SS-31 is a cationic peptide that selectively accumulates in mitochondria, particularly in the inner mitochondrial membrane, by a process that does not rely on mitochondrial membrane potential. Cardiolipin interaction: It binds to cardiolipin, a phospholipid essential for the structure and function of the inner mitochondrial membrane. Mitochondrial stabilization: By interacting with cardiolipin, SS-31 stabilizes the cristae, which are the folds of the inner membrane where ATP production occurs. Enhanced energy production: It improves the efficiency of the electron transport chain, leading to increased ATP (energy) production. Reduced oxidative stress: SS-31 inhibits the peroxidase activity of cytochrome c, which helps to prevent cardiolipin peroxidation and reduces the production of reactive oxygen species (ROS). Overall effects: The combined effects of these actions result in a restoration of mitochondrial function, which is beneficial for a wide range of conditions associated with mitochondrial dysfunction. These include improvements in energy levels, protection from cellular damage, and support for organ function in areas like the heart, kidneys, and brain.

answer:
TB-500 is a synthetic peptide that works primarily by regulating actin, a protein crucial for cell structure and movement, which in turn enhances cellular migration and promotes tissue regeneration, angiogenesis (new blood vessel formation), and inflammation modulation.

Key Mechanisms of Action

Actin Regulation and Cell Migration: TB-500 binds to G-actin monomers, preventing their polymerization into F-actin filaments. This process is essential for cell movement, allowing repair cells (like endothelial cells and keratinocytes) to rapidly migrate to sites of injury, thus accelerating wound closure and tissue repair.

Angiogenesis Promotion: The peptide stimulates the formation of new blood vessels by upregulating vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) expression and enhancing endothelial cell migration and proliferation. Improved blood flow ensures that damaged tissues receive essential oxygen and nutrients, which is vital for the healing process.

Anti-Inflammatory Modulation: TB-500 has significant anti-inflammatory properties, reducing pro-inflammatory cytokines such as TNF-α, IL-1β, and IL-6, and suppressing the activation of NF-κB. This helps create an optimal environment for healing by calming excessive inflammatory responses that could otherwise hinder recovery.

Growth Factor and Cellular Signaling Enhancement: It influences cell growth and repair by activating pathways like Akt/PI3K and enhancing HGF (hepatocyte growth factor) expression. It also supports the mobilization and differentiation of stem cells to the site of injury, providing the cellular building blocks for new tissue.

Extracellular Matrix Remodeling: TB-500 supports the formation and organization of healthy extracellular matrix components like collagen and elastin, which is essential for strong, flexible, and functional tissue repair with reduced scar formation.

Summary

TB-500's multifaceted mechanism, centered on actin modulation, allows for a systemic approach to healing across various tissues, including muscles, tendons, ligaments, skin, and even cardiac tissue in preclinical studies. It is important to note that TB-500 is an experimental therapy and is not approved for human use by the FDA. It is sold strictly for research purposes and should be used under medical supervision.

TB-500 Overview

Thymosin Beta-4 (Tβ4) is a naturally occurring 43-amino-acid peptide found in nearly all human cells. It is produced from the TMSB4X gene and is abundant in platelets, macrophages, and epithelial tissues. In laboratory research, a synthetic version called TB-500 is often used to study Tβ4's biological activity. Neither compound is approved for systemic therapeutic use; current work focuses on understanding how this peptide regulates cell movement, tissue organization, and inflammation.

answer: In what is commonly referred to as the "Wolverine Stack," BPC-157 and TB-500 are not dosed on the same schedule, even though they are often started at the same time and used synergistically. The rationale is that they appear to work through somewhat different mechanisms: BPC-157 = more localized tissue repair signaling, angiogenesis, tendon-to-bone healing, gut repair, and cellular protection. TB-500 = more systemic tissue remodeling, cell migration, connective tissue recovery, and mobility support. Typical Wolverine Stack Protocol. BPC-157: 250-500 mcg daily. Often split: 250 mcg AM, 250 mcg PM. Or 500 mcg once daily. Usually continued for 4-8 weeks. TB-500: 2-2.5 mg twice weekly. Example: Monday = 2.5 mg, Thursday = 2.5 mg. Total = 5 mg/week. Twice Weekly: TB-500: 2.5 mg Monday. TB-500: 2.5 mg Thursday. This is probably the most commonly discussed protocol among sports medicine clinics and peptide practitioners. Site-Specific vs Systemic. TB-500 injected in the abdomen, thigh, or anywhere subcutaneously. Because TB-500 is generally considered systemic, practitioners usually do not attempt site-specific administration. TB-500 provides cellular migration, tissue remodeling, new blood vessel formation, and connective tissue recovery. Together they potentially cover multiple phases of tissue healing. Practical Duration. For an athlete with a tendon or soft tissue injury: BPC-157 typically 4-8 weeks; TB-500 4-6 week loading phase; Combined Stack 4-8 weeks. If discussing the Wolverine Stack in an educational setting, the key point is that BPC-157 is typically administered daily because of its shorter activity profile and localized healing focus, while TB-500 is generally administered only once or twice weekly because of its longer systemic activity. They are started together, but they are not usually injected at the same frequency. Therefore they should be viewed as adjuncts to the fundamentals that drive recovery, including appropriate rehabilitation, progressive loading, adequate protein intake, sleep, and overall nutrition.

Systemic Injection (Non-Site-Specific) for your goal of building muscle and reducing visceral (belly) fat. filename: Tesamorelin info
answer:
Tesamorelin is FDA-approved for only one indication:
Reduction of excess abdominal visceral adipose tissue (VAT) in adults with HIV-associated lipodystrophy. It was approved under the brand name Egrifta.

What it is
Tesamorelin is a synthetic analog of growth hormone-releasing hormone (GHRH). It stimulates the pituitary gland to increase natural growth hormone (GH) secretion, which subsequently raises IGF-1 levels and promotes lipolysis (fat breakdown).

What it is NOT FDA-approved for
Tesamorelin is not FDA-approved for:
General weight loss
Obesity treatment
Athletic performance enhancement
Muscle building in healthy individuals
Anti-aging therapy
Body recomposition in the general population

Why people use it off-label
Outside its approved indication, clinicians sometimes prescribe tesamorelin off-label for:
Reduction of visceral fat in non-HIV individuals
Improvement of body composition
Support during age-related declines in GH secretion
Potential preservation of lean mass during fat-loss phases
However, these uses are based on emerging research and clinical experience rather than FDA-approved indications.

Trainer-level takeaway
Primary Use: Increases natural growth hormone release and reduces visceral abdominal fat. FDA-approved specifically for reducing excess visceral fat in adults with HIV-associated lipodystrophy.
Mechanism: Acts as a potent GHRH analog that binds pituitary GHRH receptors, increasing pulsatile GH secretion, which elevates IGF-1 and promotes preferential mobilization of visceral fat stores.

How Tesamorelin Is Typically Used
1. Systemic (Non-Site-Specific) Use
This is the standard and intended application
Used for:
Growth hormone axis stimulation
Reduction of visceral adipose tissue
Support of lean body mass retention
Metabolic and lipolytic signaling
Sleep-related GH pulse enhancement
Rationale:
Tesamorelin stimulates the pituitary gland to release GH
Effects are systemic, not localized
Mimics physiological GH pulsatility more closely than exogenous GH
Injection is never site-specific for tissue repair, unlike BPC-157.

Typical Injection Frequency
Once daily is standard
Usually administered in the evening to align with natural GH rhythms
Consistency (same time daily) is emphasized over higher dosing

Commonly Cited Dose Ranges (may vary in syringe volume with methods of reconstitution – follow supplier directions)
These reflect approved clinical use and common off-label protocols, not trainer-directed recommendations.
2 mg once daily is the FDA-approved dose (for HIV-associated lipodystrophy)
Off-label longevity / body composition protocols often range:
1–2 mg per day
Lower doses (<1 mg/day) generally show less reliable GH elevation
Unlike many peptides, Tesamorelin dosing is not usually split.

Typical Duration of Use
12–26 weeks is common in clinical and applied settings
Some protocols extend to 6–12 months under medical supervision
Effects on visceral fat and IGF-1 are gradual, not immediate
Tesamorelin is not a short-cycle peptide like BPC-157.

What Tesamorelin Is Commonly Used For
Visceral fat reduction (strongest evidence)
GH / IGF-1 axis support
Lean mass preservation during fat loss
Metabolic health support
Sleep-related recovery signaling

Mechanism of Action (Trainer-Appropriate Depth)
Tesamorelin works by:
Stimulating endogenous GH release from the pituitary
Increasing IGF-1 downstream signaling
Enhancing lipolysis, particularly in visceral fat
Preserving natural feedback loops (unlike exogenous GH)
This preserves:
Pulsatile GH secretion
Lower risk of GH suppression
Reduced likelihood of insulin resistance compared to GH injections

What Practitioners Commonly Observe (Real-World Use)
| Goal | Typical Outcome |
| Visceral fat reduction | Most consistent benefit |
| Lean mass retention | Moderate support |
| Strength gains | Indirect |
| Recovery | Subtle, cumulative |
| Sleep quality | Often improved |
Tesamorelin is not an acute performance enhancer.

Safety & Regulatory Notes (Important)
Tesamorelin is FDA-approved, but only for HIV-associated lipodystrophy
Off-label use requires medical oversight
Possible side effects include:
Water retention
Joint stiffness
Increased IGF-1
Not appropriate for:
Active malignancy
Uncontrolled diabetes
Trainers should not prescribe, source, or administer

Trainer-Friendly One-Line Explanation
“Tesamorelin helps the body release its own growth hormone more effectively, supporting fat loss and recovery without shutting down natural GH production.”

Practical Trainer / Educator Takeaway
If Tesamorelin is discussed at all, it should be positioned as:
Medical-provider–managed
Long-term and systemic
Adjunctive—not foundational
Always anchor the conversation to:
Resistance training
Sleep optimization
Protein and EAA sufficiency
Micronutrient adequacy
Load management and recovery
This keeps messaging aligned with a Playspan® / Youth-Preserving framework and avoids peptide-centric overreach.

Update product/formula
Tesamorelin is a synthetic Growth Hormone Releasing Hormone (GHRH) analog primarily used to stimulate the body’s natural pulsatile growth hormone release, which subsequently raises IGF-1 levels. Its best-studied and FDA-approved use is the reduction of excess visceral abdominal fat in HIV-associated lipodystrophy.

The standard clinically studied and FDA-approved dosage is:
2 mg subcutaneous injection once daily

The newer Egrifta WR formulation is dosed at:
1.28 mg once daily due to formulation differences and bioequivalence improvements.

Mechanistically, tesamorelin works upstream at the pituitary to increase endogenous GH secretion, which then elevates IGF-1 and promotes lipolysis, especially in visceral adipose tissue:
Clinical trials using the 2 mg/day dose demonstrated:
~14–18% reductions in visceral abdominal fat,
improvements in triglycerides and liver fat,
preservation or modest increases in lean body mass,
while having minimal effect on overall body weight.

In off-label performance/anti-aging settings, many clinics still use dosing near the original 2 mg nightly range because that is where most human efficacy data exist. Some protocols use lower doses (e.g., 0.5–1 mg/day) to reduce side effects or cost, but these lower-dose approaches are far less validated in published human research.

The most common side effects reported include:
edema/water retention,
joint pain,
tingling or numbness,
injection site reactions,
and possible insulin sensitivity changes.

source_file: 2026/Peptides HRT, & GLP FAQs  -all-2026/Women vs men IGF- blood levels -why.docx
filename: Women vs men IGF- blood levels -why
answer:
Women’s IGF-1 blood reference ranges are often listed slightly higher than men’s because of normal sex-specific physiology, not because women have “more GH” overall. The key drivers are below.

The Main Reasons Women’s IGF-1 Ranges Run Higher

1️⃣ Estrogen Enhances Hepatic IGF-1 Signaling (Context-Dependent)
IGF-1 is produced primarily in the liver in response to growth hormone (GH).
Estrogen modulates GH receptor sensitivity and downstream IGF-1 signaling.
In premenopausal women, physiologic estrogen levels:
Support efficient GH → IGF-1 coupling
Increase circulating IGF-1 binding dynamics
This can shift the population normal range slightly upward.
Important nuance: oral estrogen lowers IGF-1, while endogenous estrogen does not. Reference ranges assume typical physiology, not hormone therapy.

2️⃣ Women Secrete GH More Frequently (Pulsatility)
Women have:
More frequent GH pulses
Lower amplitude per pulse, but greater total daily GH exposure
IGF-1 reflects integrated GH exposure over time, not peak GH
Men tend to have fewer, higher GH spikes → less total daily exposure
This pulsatility difference alone explains much of the range shift.

3️⃣ Body Composition Differences
IGF-1 correlates with:
Lean mass quality
Insulin sensitivity
Metabolic efficiency
Women (especially premenopausal):
Maintain higher insulin sensitivity at equivalent BMI
Have different fat distribution (less visceral fat pre-menopause)
These factors support higher baseline IGF-1 at rest.

4️⃣ Age- and Sex-Stratified Reference Data
IGF-1 ranges are statistical, not ideal targets.
Labs stratify by:
Age
Sex
Population norms
Because healthy women cluster slightly higher, the upper and lower bounds shift upward.
This does not imply advantage or disadvantage—just different baselines.

What This Does NOT Mean
❌ Women do not have “more anabolic hormone” than men
❌ Higher IGF-1 does not automatically mean better muscle gain
❌ Men with IGF-1 in the female range are not abnormal
Muscle hypertrophy is still driven primarily by:
Androgens
Mechanical tension
Nutrition
Recovery

Trainer / Client-Friendly One-Liner
“Women often have slightly higher normal IGF-1 ranges because estrogen and growth hormone work together differently—it's a normal, healthy sex difference, not a problem or advantage.”

Practical Interpretation Tip
Always interpret IGF-1 relative to age and sex, not across genders.
More important than the absolute number:
Trends over time
Symptoms
Context (sleep, nutrition, training load, hormone status)
topics: sex differences in GH and IGF-1

Q: There is no protein listed on AminoFormula (AF), can I count it as a protein?

A: You may add 25-40gm (1-2scoops) of protein to your daily protein intake when using AF as directed, but generally no more regardless of daily intake. The reason AminoFormula (AF) does not publish a protein amount is because it is purposely not a complete protein as it contains only the essential amino acids that are directly responsible for protein synthesis activation and therefore serves as a low calorie, fast acting, high anabolic signaling product for activating muscle protein synthesis (MPS) beyond intact protein itself. Your total food/shake protein intake throughout the day supplies the remaining amino acids (and can be made in the body) necessary for the complete and prolonged synthesis. That said, AF can be used to fortify a low protein meal/food (e.g., plant based, low protein breakfast etc.,) to raise the total food protein biological (BV) - i.e., eliminate the AA limiting factor for MPS indigenous to weaker protein sources. Further, AF is vegan friendly.

More info:

AF serves to enhance the MPS process beyond protein alone or serve as a low calorie, high anabolic extra source of protein. A protein equivalent in 1-scoop of AF, is generally counted as ~25gms, as it takes ~25-35gms of a complete protein to get the amount of the EAA found in one serving of AF including the 6gms of BCAA. However, regardless of your total AF intake, we advise you only add it as 25-40gm of protein to your 1gm/LB/lean body mass(LBM)/day of protein needs. Mindful that active strength/performance athletes still maintain the 1gm/LB/LBM/D of whole/intact protein sources because different whole food protein has other helpful properties/nutrients including satiety.

question_original: I have a client who is post partum and currently breast feeding. Her goal is longevity and weight loss. What supplements would be safe to recommend for her?
question_canonical: Which supplements are safe to recommend for a postpartum client who is breastfeeding and has longevity and weight loss goals?
answer:
Hi [CUSTOMER],

Thanks for contacting us. The list of supplements that are commonly used and safe during pregnancy and/or breastfeeding is below.

The weight loss piece needs to be approached carefully with a breastfeeding client. Aggressive calorie restriction can affect milk supply and nutrient density of breast milk. The goal should be gradual, sustainable fat loss, not a hard cut.

A few things that are off the table for now:
- ThermAccel / any stimulant-based thermogenic: not appropriate while breastfeeding, full stop.
- CarbRepel: skip it for now; not the right tool during this phase.
- WeightLoss & LiverSupport: hold off until she's done breastfeeding; better to be conservative here.

The foundational stack (baseline dietary support): multivitamin, omega-3, calcium, and a clean protein source, is not only safe, it's arguably more important now than at any other time in her life. Her nutrient demands are elevated while breastfeeding, and a calorie-controlled diet makes hitting those daily targets even harder.

Thanks again and have great day!

Supplements that are ok during pregnancy, trying to conceive or breastfeeding: the dotFIT Women’s multivitamin and mineral formula (Women’sMV during breastfeeding or trying to conceive, but use the doctor prescribed prenatal during pregnancy), additional Vitamin D, SuperOmega-3s, any of the meal replacements, or protein mixes/shakes and nutrition bars (such as LeanMeal, WheySmooth, etc.,); and if needed, SuperCalcium and extra iron by doctors recommendation. If you prefer a protein supplement that is completely natural, use the All Natural WheySmooth or the BestPlantProtein (all plant protein/vegan).

*The California Prop 65 lead standards are unrealistic in natural foods and disputed globally, because almost all foods contain amounts higher than allowed lead/metals (.5mcg/svg) including 1 svg natural spinach (10X higher), 1-cup of coffee, etc. This is because the level is set 10-50 times lower than other global (e.g., FDA [2.2mcg/d children; 12.5 adults], NSF, WHO, etc.) limits for lead (5-30mcg). Based on the unrealistic levels, almost all plant foods would be prohibited.
More information
From Council of Responsible Nutrition: "Prop 65 levels are not meant to represent a safety threshold or a cut-off for unsafe levels, but rather, a standard that triggers a label notification only in the state of California to inform consumers which products contain metals, which are naturally present in most natural sources of food and water. To put this into context, a 1/2 cup of cooked spinach would require a Prop 65 warning label, if they were required for wholefoods, which they are not."

source_file: 2026/Protein-muscle full effect total-.18-.25.docx
filename: Protein-muscle full effect total-.18-.25
answer:
Question #4: How Much Protein Can I Handle in a Single Meal?
This is really two questions:
How much protein do I need to maximally stimulate protein synthesis?
Is it true that anything beyond that amount is a waste?
We’ll start with the second question because [NAME] hears it from patients way more often than he’d like to.
“I tell them, no, it’s not a waste,” he said. Even if the patient has fully engaged protein synthesis, there’s a lot more going on. The total amount of daily protein in your diet and the quality of that protein matter more than how much you eat at any particular meal.
For the first question, [NAME] has three answers:
In younger adults, about 0.25 g of high-quality protein per kilogram of body weight per meal should adequately stimulate protein synthesis. That assumes the protein contains 2-3 g of leucine.
Older adults who have some resistance to leucine should aim for 0.4 g per kilogram per meal.
Maximum protein stimulation should occur with roughly 0.4-0.55 g per kilogram.
Put simply, 20 g of protein per meal should get the party started for a younger adult, 30 g should work for an older adult, and 40 g should maximally engage protein synthesis for almost anyone.
But again, higher amounts of protein at one meal aren’t “wasted.”
In fact, a 2023 study found that 100 g of protein stimulated more protein synthesis over the next 12 hours than 25 g.
Nobody is suggesting you should consume 100 g of protein in any meal. Even if we thought it was a good idea, few of us could choke down 1.2 pounds of beef, two large chicken breasts, or 16 eggs at one sitting.
The point to make to your patients is this: Consume the nutrients your body needs, and your body will figure out what to do with them.

filename: Psyllium husk info
answer:
For general health, cholesterol reduction, blood sugar control, and digestive regularity, the most commonly studied dose of psyllium husk is:

Typical Effective Doses

General digestive health / regularity: 3–5 grams, 1–2 times daily. Total daily intake: 5–10 grams.

Cholesterol reduction: 5–7 grams, twice daily. Total daily intake: 10–14 grams/day. Often taken before or with meals.

Blood sugar support: 5 grams taken 15–30 minutes before meals. Total daily intake: 10–15 grams/day.

Weight management / satiety: 5–10 grams mixed in water, 15–30 minutes before meals. Total daily intake: 10–15 grams/day.

Practical Translation

Psyllium husk powders vary slightly by density, but generally:
1 teaspoon ≈ 3–4 grams
1 tablespoon ≈ 7–10 grams

Therefore:
A typical maintenance dose is 1 teaspoon twice daily.
A common therapeutic dose for cholesterol and blood sugar management is 1 tablespoon twice daily.

Important Considerations

Always take with at least 8–12 oz (240–360 mL) of water.
Start low (e.g., 3–5 g/day) and increase over 1–2 weeks to minimize gas and bloating.
Separate from medications and supplements by 1–2 hours, since psyllium can reduce absorption of some compounds.

Takeaway

For most healthy adults, 5 grams twice daily (10 g/day total) is a practical, evidence-based dose that provides meaningful benefits for digestive health, LDL cholesterol reduction, blood sugar control, and satiety without requiring very large amounts. For those specifically targeting cholesterol lowering, 10–14 grams/day is where many of the strongest clinical benefits have been observed.

source_file: 2026/Reverse dieting.docx
filename: Reverse dieting
question_original: Hello! I was wondering if Neal and Zane have ever done a podcast on reverse dieting? I trust their knowledge and advice, and I keep hearing conflicting arguments and I’m not sure which resources to trust, or how to research this correctly on my own. THANK YOU for sharing your knowledge!
question_canonical: Has the dotFIT team ever done a podcast on reverse dieting, and how can I research this topic reliably on my own?
answer:
Hi [CUSTOMER],

Thanks for contacting us and digging for the facts through the SuppBeast.

Honestly, a lot of the confusion around ‘reverse dieting’ comes from the name itself because it makes it sound like some new or special fat-loss strategy when it’s really not. Reverse dieting originally came from the bodybuilding world (me included) after extremely restrictive contest diets, where calories were brought back up slowly to avoid rapid rebound fat gain while returning to a more sustainable intake. For example, if a competitor had dieted down to 1,500 calories for a show, they might gradually increase by 100–150 calories per week until they found their maintenance level without suddenly overeating (and of course our exercise output was changing dramatically after the competition as well - so that was factoring onto the calorie intake as well). That’s all reverse dieting really is — a controlled return to maintenance calories after aggressive dieting.

Today, social media often presents reverse dieting as some sort of metabolism-hacking magic method, but the science really doesn’t support that idea. It doesn’t suddenly ‘repair’ metabolism or allow people to eat unlimited calories without gaining body fat. What it can do is help someone transition out of a restrictive diet in a more structured and psychologically controlled way and hey, as the calories go up, the person may want to be more active helping them burn more calories. So, for most healthy exercisers and gym members, the focus should be less on chasing trendy terms like ‘reverse dieting’ and more on building sustainable eating habits, adequate protein intake, resistance training, and maintaining a calorie level that supports the immediate goal and then the long-term results without extremes.

So your quick takeaway is that “Reverse dieting” isn’t a magic metabolism trick — it’s simply a gradual return to maintenance calories after aggressive dieting to help minimize rebound weight gain and regain a sustainable eating pattern. The real long-term success still comes from consistent nutrition habits, adequate protein, resistance training, and avoiding extreme dieting in the first place.

Hope this helps and thanks for listening to facts as they unfold on all things nutrition and weight control on the SuppBeast.

Have a great weekend.

filename: Turkesterone
answer:
Recent studies on turkesterone show mixed results, with limited, often conflicting evidence in human trials regarding muscle growth and performance improvements. While some studies suggest it may aid in recovery or provide subtle ergogenic effects, recent 2024-2025 research indicates no significant increases in lean muscle mass, muscle strength, or metabolic rate compared to placebos.

Key Findings on Turkesterone Studies:

Muscle Growth/Performance: A 2025 study found no significant changes in body composition, strength, or power in participants over 4 weeks. Earlier studies suggested potential, but more robust human research is needed.

Safety & Side Effects: Studies show doses up to 2,000 mg are generally well-tolerated with no significant adverse impacts on blood pressure, heart rate, or liver function. Minor issues like nausea or stomach discomfort may occur.

Mechanism: As a phytoecdysteroid, it is thought to act on muscle cells through pathways different from traditional steroids, focusing on protein synthesis stimulation rather than androgen receptor binding.

Long-Term Effects: Data on the long-term effects of turkesterone use is virtually non-existent, leaving its long-term safety profile unknown.

Legality in Sports: It is currently not banned in sports, though similar ecdysteroids are on the WADA monitoring list.

YouTube +1

Conclusion of Current Research

The majority of studies supporting high efficacy are in animals (rodents) or cell cultures, with human data still in its infancy. Although safe, studies to date fail to definitively support its effectiveness as a potent, natural anabolic agent for muscle growth.

3.5. Turkesterone and Ajuga turkestanica

Turkesterone is a PE, with 27 carbon atoms and seven OH-groups; it is considered that the OH groups at C-20 and C-11 are responsible for the anabolic effects [28,215]. Turkesterone is considered to possess an anabolic effect, and it is used as DS by athletes, instead of anabolic steroids [28,30]. It is found in some endemic plants, such as A. turkestanica, R. carthamoides, Triticum aestivum L., Vitex scabra, etc. [13,69,216,217,218]. The highest content of turkesterone is considered to be in Ajuga turkestanica [19]. Moreover, in DSs, turkesterone is derived from A. turkestanica [28].

Ecdysteroid-enriched preparations of A. turkestanica (or pure turkesterone) exhibit anabolic effects [216,219,220].

Ajuga turkestanica, a plant species of the Lamiaceae family, grows wild in the Boysun mountainous region of Central Asia, Uzbekistan. It is a perennial plant, that normally grows on clay, petrous, and rubbly slopes and rocks, with a height of 40–60 cm [14]. Both the aerial parts and root sections are utilized in folk medicine to prevent obesity, hair loss, and gastrointestinal diseases [14,216].

The phytochemical profile of A. turkestanica has indicated the existence of several biologically active secondary metabolites, such as carbohydrates, iridoids, diterpenes, phytoecdysteroids, flavonoids, sterol glycosides, and phenylethanoid glycosides [14,53,216]. The A. turkestanica extract contained 2.1% (w/w) turkesterone and 0.9% (w/w) 20HE [19]. Other isolated Pes are cyasterone, ajugasterone B, α-ecdysone, ecdysone 2,3-monoacetonide, and 22-acetylcyasterone [59,221,222].

Extracts from A. turkestanica are associated with wound-healing effects [223], as well as antiproliferative, anti-stress and immunostimulating, antimicrobial, and antioxidant effects [12,59]. Most of these effects are likely due to the presence of Pes [224]. Table 9 presents studies about the biological effects of turkesterone. Ajuga turkestanica and turkesterone products are commercially available not only online but also in bodybuilding centers [12]. The studies presented in the tables reported the various effects of turkesterone and A. turkestanica. Turkesterone is associated with a reduction in lipid accumulation in human adipocytes [69]. In a stress-induced mouse model, ecdysterone and turkesterone were found to prevent stress-related consequences and restore immunological activity [138]. Additionally, turkesterone exhibited beneficial effects on the endocrine and exocrine function in alloxan-induced diabetic rats, suggesting its potential therapeutic application in diabetes management [225]. Furthermore, PEs from A. turkestanica demonstrate hypoglycemic activity in models of hyperglycemia and diabetes, suggesting their potential therapeutic use in managing blood glucose levels [227]. Turkesterone presents a safer option to conventional anabolic steroids, displaying significant anabolic effects without inducing androgenic side effects in in vivo animal studies [19,219]. Moreover, A. turkestanica also enhances muscle regeneration and maintenance [29,226]. These results suggest that turkesterone extracted from A. turkestanica possesses diverse physiological effects, including potential performance enhancement and antiadipogenic, immunomodulatory, and hypoglycemic activities, making it a promising candidate for sports nutrition. Further research is needed to fully understand the mechanisms of action and therapeutic potential of turkesterone and A. turkestanica [19,29,59,69,77,138,219,220,225,226,227].

4. Conclusions

Phytoecdysteroids, widely distributed across various plant species, have been valued for their adaptogenic properties and potential to enhance muscle strength and performance. 20-hydroxyecdysone and turkesterone are two of the most noteworthy PEs, which are found in plants such as R. carthamoides, S. oleracea, C. quinoa, and A. turkestanica. Nowadays, these plants are used not just in plant-based diets for their high nutritional value but also as major components of DSs. Since 2020, ecdysterone has garnered attention and has been included in the WADA’s monitoring program due to its ability to enhance physical endurance. Studies on the benefits of 20HE, turkesterone, and extracts from these plants are limited. The preparations from these plants show promise not only as nutritional supplements but also as therapeutic agents for treating medicinal disorders, such as chronic tiredness, heart disorders, and neurodegenerative diseases. Future double-blind randomized multicenter trials are critical for fully assessing the effectiveness and safety of these preparations for cardiovascular disease, chronic tiredness, obesity, and osteoporosis. These studies will provide valuable insights into the therapeutic potential of phytoecdysteroid-rich extracts.

What is turkesterone?

Turkesterone is a type of ecdysteroid, a steroid-like compound found in certain plants and insects. The supplement form is commonly sourced from Ajuga turkestanica. Unlike anabolic-androgenic steroids, turkesterone is not thought to work by binding to the androgen receptor the way testosterone or Dianabol would.

In plain English: it’s often marketed as “anabolic without the steroid side effects,” but that claim depends on whether it actually produces meaningful muscle/strength outcomes in humans.

Does turkesterone work? What the best human studies show

Here’s the key point: the most relevant evidence is human trials measuring body composition and performance. And the most direct turkesterone supplementation studies we have right now are short (4 weeks) and generally show no meaningful advantage vs placebo.

Human study #1: 500 mg/day turkesterone for 4 weeks (DXA body comp)

A 2024 study randomized active men and women to 500 mg/day turkesterone or placebo for 4 weeks and measured changes via DXA. Result: no significant differences in body mass, lean mass, fat mass, or body fat percentage compared to placebo.

Human study #2: “turkesterone-containing product” (Turk Builder®) for 4 weeks

A 2025 randomized, double-blind trial tested a turkesterone-containing product for 4 weeks and tracked body composition, handgrip strength, mood, and sleep. Result: no significant differences between treatment and placebo groups across those measures.

Acute study: multiple doses and short-term markers

A 2024 preliminary study looked at acute dosing and markers like IGF-1 and resting metabolic rate over a short window. It did not find statistically significant effects, though it notes the work is “foundational” for future research.

Bottom line from human trials so far:

If you’re expecting obvious hypertrophy or strength jumps in a month, current human studies suggest you’ll likely be disappointed.

Study snapshot table (for quick scanning)

| Study | Design | Dose / Duration | What they measured | Result |
| [NAME] et al. (2024) | Randomized, placebo-controlled | 500 mg/day, 4 weeks | DXA body composition | No significant change vs placebo |
| [NAME] et al. (2025) | Double-blind, placebo-controlled | Turk Builder® 1 cap/day, 4 weeks | Body comp, handgrip, mood, sleep | No significant differences vs placebo |
| [NAME] et al. (2024) | Acute dosing study | Multiple doses, short time window | IGF-1, RMR, metabolic markers | No significant effects; exploratory |
| [NAME] et al. (2019) (ecdysterone) | Training intervention (ecdysterone) | 10 weeks (varied dosing) | Performance / training outcomes | Suggestive effects, but different compound & context |

How might turkesterone work? (Mechanism)

Ecdysteroids are hypothesized to influence pathways related to muscle protein synthesis, energy metabolism, and recovery. A 2024 review summarizes proposed mechanisms (protein synthesis support, ATP-related effects, and other metabolic influences), but also makes clear that mechanisms are still being clarified and don’t guarantee real-world hypertrophy.

Key takeaway: A plausible mechanism can be interesting, but users ultimately care about outcomes, and current human outcomes are not impressive.

Turkesterone benefits: what’s realistic?

Muscle gain: Not convincingly supported by current short-term human trials.

Strength/performance: No clear improvements in the direct turkesterone trials; ecdysterone research is a different bucket.

Recovery/“feel” effects: Mostly anecdotal—hard to separate from placebo without longer, larger trials.

Turkesterone dosage (what people use vs what studies used)

Many supplement brands recommend around 500 mg/day, commonly split into 1–2 doses. That’s also the dose used in one of the most direct 4-week trials.

If you insist on trying it:

Use a consistent dose daily for 6–8 weeks (longer than most studies),

Track body weight, waist, lifts, sleep, and training volume,

Don’t change 10 variables at once (diet + training + 6 new supplements),

Stop if you experience side effects.

Turkesterone side effects & safety

Direct long-term safety data in humans is limited. However, broader ecdysteroid literature often describes a favorable safety profile in mammals and summarizes toxicology background.

That said, athletes should also understand regulatory context: ecdysteroids are not currently prohibited, but are on WADA’s monitoring list (meaning it’s being tracked and could change in the future).

Commonly reported issues are usually mild (e.g., GI discomfort), but high-quality data is sparse. If you’re pregnant/nursing, have a medical condition, or take medications, talk to a qualified healthcare professional first.

FDA disclaimer: These statements have not been evaluated by the Food and Drug Administration. This content is for educational purposes and is not medical advice.

Turkesterone vs creatine (and what you should take instead)

If your goal is to build muscle and get stronger, creatine monohydrate is still the king because it has a much larger, higher-quality evidence base than turkesterone. If you’re choosing where to spend money, creatine + protein + total calories + training progression will almost always beat “hype” supplements.
